case_studies.title: Student Voice — Bilingual Cohort Feedback & Voting Platform
case_studies.subtitle: Eliminating language and privacy barriers in university cohort communications
case_studies.problem: Cohort communication in the UWE Data Science & AI degree was held almost entirely in informal WhatsApp groups. International Chinese-speaking students faced language friction, many peers hesitated to raise sensitive module issues because their private phone numbers were visible to everyone, and feedback was lost in endless casual chat without any prioritisation for the course committee.
case_studies.role_and_approach: As Student Representative, I ran a requirements discovery exercise with fellow students. I mapped the broken AS-IS communication flow against a streamlined TO-BE platform model. I authored formal BA documentation including functional requirements, user stories with acceptance criteria, and a UAT test matrix covering anonymous submissions, server-side translation, and content moderation.
steps_taken: Conducted discovery sessions with domestic and international students to identify feedback barriers.
Produced AS-IS vs TO-BE workflow diagrams in Miro highlighting drop-off points in WhatsApp groups.
Drafted functional specifications for 3 personas: Student (anonymous submitter/voter), Student Rep (consolidator/liaison), and Course Leader (reviewer).
Built and launched a responsive, mobile-first web application with single-tap English and Simplified Chinese switching (EN / 中文).
Implemented frictionless zero-account submission with server-side rate limiting and HMAC voter token hashing to preserve anonymity.
Configured atomic Firestore transactions to prevent duplicate voting while strictly prohibiting direct client-side database writes.
Built a password-protected administrative console with instant QR code generator for in-person lecture hall feedback rounds.
case_studies.outcome: Eliminated contact-sharing fears and language barriers across the cohort. Enabled students to submit and vote on module issues in under 30 seconds. Elevated cohort participation and provided structured, priority-ranked evidence directly to university faculty during Student-Staff Liaison Committee meetings.

case_studies.title: Capital Bikeshare — Operations & Fleet Demand Analytics Dashboard
case_studies.subtitle: Interactive operational intelligence across 17,379 hourly rental records
case_studies.problem: Fleet rebalancing teams in Washington D.C. struggle with contrasting demand profiles: high-volume commuter surges on weekdays versus unpredictable weather-dependent leisure rides on weekends. Operations managers needed a responsive dashboard to quickly spot peak hourly load and seasonal patterns without navigating static spreadsheet reports.
case_studies.role_and_approach: Acted as Product Analyst and UI Architect. Formulated user personas for Fleet Logistics Coordinators and Regional Operations Managers. Translated raw UCI Bike Sharing records (17,379 hourly logs over 731 operational days) into an executive visual dashboard with real-time dynamic filtering.
steps_taken: Audited the source dataset (UCI Bike Sharing) and established key business metrics: Total Trips, Daily Average, Registered/Casual Split, and Weather Severity Impact.
Designed the visual information architecture: primary KPI cards at the top, a semi-circular radial gauge for user mix, followed by multi-dimensional time series.
Constructed a 168-cell 24-Hour × 7-Day Demand Heatmap to expose commuter peaks (08:00 and 17:00 weekdays) versus mid-day weekend leisure volume.
Implemented instant client-side multi-filter controls (Year: All, 2011, 2012; Day Type: All, Working Days, Weekends/Holidays) with zero backend latency.
Conducted UI responsiveness testing across desktop, tablet, and mobile displays.
case_studies.outcome: Delivered a lightweight, zero-dependency operations tool hosted on GitHub Pages. Proved that registered commuters represent ~81% of all trips with sharp commuter spikes, allowing operations teams to plan van-based bike relocations accurately before 07:30 AM.

case_studies.title: Explainable AI Text Classifier — Transparent Stylometric Analysis
case_studies.subtitle: Replacing black-box AI detection scores with transparent, accountable writing metrics
case_studies.problem: Commercial AI detection tools (Turnitin, GPTZero, Undetectable AI) present high-stakes percentage scores without explaining how the decision was reached. Studies (Liang et al., 2023) show these tools disproportionately flag non-native English students as AI simply for using formal grammar, leading to unwarranted academic penalties.
case_studies.role_and_approach: Conducted academic research and built a transparent prototype for my UWE Data Science & AI degree project. Rather than treating detection as an opaque neural network, I designed an interpretable pipeline that evaluates 7 measurable, length-invariant writing habits and uses TreeSHAP to reveal exactly how each habit pulled the score up or down.
steps_taken: Selected and cleaned Kaggle's DAIGT-V2 dataset containing 44,868 essays (27,371 human essays and 17,497 AI generations from ChatGPT, GPT-4, Claude, PaLM, LLaMA, and Mistral).

Engineered 7 length-invariant stylometric features: sentence length variation, average sentence length, commas per 100w, transition words per 100w, average word length, semicolons/colons, and punctuation density.
Trained a Random Forest classifier using prompt-grouped 80/20 train/test splitting, ensuring the model was tested strictly on unseen topics.
Integrated the TreeSHAP library to calculate exact local feature attributions, explaining the contribution of each individual writing habit.
Embedded prominent ethical caveats on the interface, advising educators that no stylometric model is 100% infallible and must never be used alone to penalise students.
artifacts_produced: Ethical Risk Assessment & Misuse Prevention Guidelines
Confusion Matrix & Held-Out Test Evaluation Report (83.1% Accuracy, 4.4% Human FPR at 0.60 threshold)
case_studies.outcome: Demonstrated how machine learning models can be made explainable and auditable in high-stakes educational contexts, providing transparent evidence rather than opaque percentage probabilities.

case_studies.title: Bristol Road Safety Explorer — DfT Police Collision Analytics
case_studies.subtitle: Spatial hotspot grouping and multi-table collision analysis for highway safety officers
case_studies.problem: UK Department for Transport (DfT) road casualty data spans millions of records with separate tables for collisions, vehicles, and casualties. Safety officers evaluating Bristol roads often struggled with relational grain multiplication and unclear changes in reporting systems (such as Avon & Somerset's 2025 transition to injury-based reporting).
case_studies.role_and_approach: Architected an exploratory browser dashboard that processes raw DfT open datasets into an intuitive spatial investigation platform for road safety inspectors, complete with plain-English methodology documentation.
steps_taken: Resolved complex relational grain: separated distinct collision counts from casualty headcounts to prevent Cartesian join inflation.
Implemented DBSCAN spatial clustering with a 25-metre neighbourhood radius to identify candidate repeat collision clusters without relying on arbitrary boundary lines.
Built interactive Leaflet street maps, weekday-by-hour collision heatmaps, and casualty circumstance breakdowns.
Compiled thorough QA documentation (VALIDATION.md) disclosing source data limitations, unrecorded codes, and Avon & Somerset police reporting shifts.
case_studies.outcome: Created a zero-dependency standalone dashboard that lets safety officers inspect repeat-incident clusters, cross-filter by vehicle and road user types, and export clean subsets for field inspection.

case_studies.title: AI Image-Prompt Platform — Retention & Supply Funnel Analysis
case_studies.subtitle: Using behavioral analytics to turn 10,000 monthly visitors into active contributors
case_studies.problem: An early-stage AI prompt sharing community attracted strong monthly traffic (~10,000 unique visitors), but user behavior was overwhelmingly passive: visitors copied prompts but rarely contributed new ones, threatening community sustainability.
case_studies.role_and_approach: Conducted an end-to-end product funnel and user session analysis to uncover why readers dropped off without submitting content.
steps_taken: Analysed user session replays and scroll heatmaps using Google Analytics and Microsoft Clarity.
Identified key friction points: an intimidating multi-field submission form and a total lack of creator incentives or recognition.
Proposed a two-sided value proposition: introduced creator monetization options and public contributor profile badges.
Streamlined the prompt contribution form, reducing mandatory input fields by 50%.
case_studies.outcome: Onboarded 16 independent creator sellers who began contributing exclusive prompt sets regularly, transforming a one-way consumer site into a bilateral community.
